extracted.intended_audience: historians and philosophers of science; scientists and graduate students interested in scientific method and the nature of discovery
extracted.subtask_description: Framework and evaluative criteria for understanding how paradigms shape normal science, how discoveries arise (anomaly, assimilation, paradigm change), and how instruments, procedures, and specialization affect recognition of novel phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigms guide research by direct modeling as well as through abstracted rules
rubrics_metrics.description: “These consequences of scientific education have a converse that provides a third reason to suppose that paradigms guide research by direct modeling as well as through abstracted rules.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paradigms function not only as explicit rules but as models (exemplars) that scientists imitate; practitioners often cannot articulate field-wide rules but show paradigm knowledge through successful research practice. When paradigms feel insecure, explicit rule-seeking and methodological debates increase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigms can be local to specialties / need not be common across a whole profession
rubrics_metrics.description: “Explicit rules, when they exist, are usually common to a very broad scientific group, but paradigms need not be. ... What quantum mechanics means to each of them depends upon what courses he has had, what texts he has read, and which journals he studies.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a purported paradigm is shared across the whole field or is particular to a subspecialty; changes in a paradigm application may be revolutionary for some subgroups but not for others (examples: different applications of quantum mechanics; helium atom judged differently by chemist vs physicist).

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal science does not aim at novelties of fact or theory
rubrics_metrics.description: “Normal science, the puzzle-solving activity we have just examined, is a highly cumulative enterprise ... Yet one standard product of the scientific enterprise is missing. Normal science does not aim at novelties of fact or theory and, when successful, finds none.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate research as 'normal science' when its goals are extension, precision, and problem-solving within an accepted paradigm rather than seeking revolutionary novelties; nevertheless, surprises can and do arise from normal-science activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery commences with the awareness of anomaly
rubrics_metrics.description: “Discovery commences with the awareness of anomaly, i.e., with the recognition that nature has somehow violated the paradigm-induced expectations that govern normal science.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing or conducting research, identify anomalies—observations that conflict with paradigm-induced expectations—as the typical starting point for discovery; the recognition of anomaly triggers investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery requires exploration and assimilation; it closes only when theory adjusted so anomalous becomes expected
rubrics_metrics.description: “It then continues with a more or less extended exploration of the area of anomaly. And it closes only when the paradigm theory has been adjusted so that the anomalous has become the expected.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat discovery as an extended process: observation of anomaly → exploration/experimentation → theoretical adjustment/assimilation. A putative discovery is not complete until conceptual categories have been altered so the anomaly is incorporated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery is a process, not a single instant; involves both seeing that and seeing what
rubrics_metrics.description: “Discovering, like seeing or touching, should be unequivocally attributable to an individual and to a moment in time. But the latter attribution is always impossible ... discovering a new sort of phenomenon is necessarily a complex event, one which involves recognizing both that something is and what it is.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assigning discovery to a single moment or person without caveats; analyses of priority and dating must account for the gradual intertwining of observation and conceptualization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance of a phenomenon varies with the extent it violated paradigm-induced anticipations
rubrics_metrics.description: “The value placed upon a new phenomenon and thus upon its discoverer varies with our estimate of the extent to which the phenomenon violated paradigm-induced anticipations.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating the importance of a result, consider how much it conflicts with existing paradigm expectations—greater conflict often corresponds to higher perceived significance and to likelihood of paradigm change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advance awareness of theoretical difficulties predisposes individuals to make discoveries
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: Lavoisier had earlier been convinced something was wrong with phlogiston theory and recorded a sealed note in 1772; this advance awareness enabled him to interpret experiments leading to oxygen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether investigators had prior theoretical dissatisfaction or puzzles that made them receptive to anomalous data; pre-existing skepticism can be crucial in recognizing and interpreting anomalies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accidental (serendipitous) discovery is common — notice unexpected effects in routine work
rubrics_metrics.description: X-rays: Roentgen noticed a barium platino-cyanide screen glowing at some distance from shielded apparatus; that accidental observation started a seven-week investigation culminating in discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain vigilance for unexpected observations during routine experiments; follow-up systematic investigation of surprising effects is essential—many who saw the initial effect did not pursue it and so missed the discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrumental and procedural commitments embed expectations and can blind investigators
rubrics_metrics.description: “The decision to employ a particular piece of apparatus and to use it in a particular way carries an assumption that only certain sorts of circumstances will arise. There are instrumental as well as theoretical expectations ...” Examples: Priestley’s standard nitric-oxide test; failure to detect fission products because tests targeted upper periodic-table elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how standard instruments, tests, and procedures might limit the range of detectable phenomena; consider whether alternate procedures or different proportions/tests could reveal anomalies missed by orthodox methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigm procedures are necessary despite restricting effects
rubrics_metrics.description: “Ought we conclude ... that science should abandon standard tests and standard instruments? That would result in an inconceivable method of research. Paradigm procedures and applications are as necessary to science as paradigm laws and theories ...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance critique of procedural blindness with recognition that standard methods enable cumulative, repeatable research; remedy is not abandonment but awareness and targeted probing for anomalous conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory-induced discoveries: speculative/tentative theories can point to discoveries but require experimental articulation
rubrics_metrics.description: “Often, however, that discovery is not quite the one anticipated by the speculative and tentative hypothesis. Only as experiment and tentative theory are together articulated to a match does the discovery emerge and the theory become a paradigm.” (Leyden jar example)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When hypotheses are speculative, expect iterative back-and-forth between experiment and theory; successful articulation can convert tentative ideas into new paradigms—evaluate the fit between data and the evolving theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common characteristics of discoveries (explicit list)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Those characteristics include: the previous awareness of anomaly, the gradual and simultaneous emergence of both observational and conceptual recognition, and the consequent change of paradigm categories and procedures often accompanied by resistance.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these three characteristics as a checklist when analyzing historical or contemporary discoveries: (1) was there an antecedent sense of anomaly? (2) did observation and conceptual recognition emerge together over time? (3) did assimilation require changes in categories/procedures and provoke resistance?

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception/recognition is shaped by expectations (psychological constraint on discovery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference to Bruner and Postman experiment showing that subjects’ identification of playing cards depended on expectations; anomalies (e.g., a red six of spades) are harder to perceive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for cognitive/perceptual biases when evaluating reports of anomalies or failed recognitions; paradigm-induced perceptual habits can prevent immediate detection of anomalous phenomena.
